reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A terminal deletion of the long arm of chromosome 18, most often de novo and of variable size rather than a single recurrent rearrangement
Developmental delay and mild to moderate intellectual disability with short stature, sometimes related to growth hormone deficiency
Hearing loss is characteristic and frequently linked to narrowing or atresia of the external auditory canals
Brain MRI often shows abnormal or delayed myelination (dysmyelination), which can correlate with neurological findings
Hypotonia, foot deformities and variable facial dysmorphism are common
Immune abnormalities, particularly IgA deficiency, occur and may predispose to infection
Phenotype and severity vary with the size and breakpoint of the deletion
Chromosomal microarray defines the deletion and its extent
reference.pathophysiology: Distal 18q deletion syndrome results from loss of the terminal long arm of chromosome 18, usually as a de novo terminal deletion of variable size, though unbalanced translocations also occur. It behaves as a contiguous-gene syndrome in which haploinsufficiency of multiple dosage-sensitive genes produces the neurodevelopmental, growth, auditory and immune features. Loss of genes influencing myelination is thought to contribute to the white-matter changes seen on imaging. The variability in deletion size and breakpoint largely accounts for the range of clinical severity.
additionalDifferentials: Proximal (interstitial) 18q deletion syndrome, which has a distinct phenotype
Other subtelomeric or terminal deletion syndromes
Syndromic causes of conductive hearing loss with aural atresia
Leukodystrophies and other causes of abnormal myelination on MRI
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as the first-line test to detect and size the terminal deletion
FISH or MLPA to confirm the deletion and assess for a parental rearrangement
Parental studies to exclude an inherited translocation and guide recurrence-risk counselling
Audiological assessment and imaging of the external and middle ear
Brain MRI to evaluate myelination and structural anomalies
Growth monitoring with endocrine evaluation for growth hormone deficiency, and immunoglobulin assessment
redFlags: Significant hearing loss impairing communication and development
Faltering growth suggesting growth hormone deficiency
Recurrent or severe infection raising concern about immune deficiency
Seizures or neurological deterioration requiring evaluation
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability and can achieve meaningful function with early support, particularly when hearing loss is identified and managed and growth is optimised. Long-term outlook depends on the severity of the developmental, auditory and immune involvement, which correlates broadly with deletion size.
pitfalls: Missing conductive hearing loss and aural atresia that compound developmental difficulty
Overlooking growth hormone deficiency as a treatable cause of short stature
Failing to recognise IgA deficiency and other immune problems predisposing to infection
Confusing the distal deletion with the proximal 18q deletion, which differs clinically
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Provide early developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, and educational support for intellectual disability
Identify and manage hearing loss with audiological assessment, hearing aids, and ENT input for external auditory canal atresia or stenosis
Monitor growth and evaluate for growth hormone deficiency, offering growth hormone therapy where confirmed
Assess immune function and manage IgA deficiency with prompt treatment of infections
Manage foot deformities and hypotonia with orthopaedic and physiotherapy input
Follow up neurologically with brain MRI to characterise dysmyelination-related changes
Offer genetic counselling with parental studies to determine recurrence risk and exclude an inherited translocation
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary follow-up team
